query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion is governed by the dynamic formation and maintenance of a mechanically adaptive passive film. This film, which is sustained by the unique multicomponent microstructure of HEAs, continuously reforms by leveraging minor phase transformations at the wear interface to provide enhanced passivation during mechanical degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: An equimolar or near-equimolar high-entropy alloy with a predominantly single-phase (e.g., FCC) matrix and a metastable microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA samples to combined tribocorrosion tests where controlled mechanical wear is applied concurrently with exposure to a corrosive environment (e.g., saline solution), and compare with tests under isolated wear and isolated corrosion conditions.
generation.conditions: Tests should be performed at ambient temperature under constant loading and wear rate with a fixed concentration of corrosive electrolyte. A matched baseline of the same HEA under only corrosion or only wear conditions will be used for comparison.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuously regenerating passive film, whose composition and nanostructure are influenced by minor phase transformations and localized oxidation, mediates the improved resistance.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear exposes fresh surfaces that rapidly repassivate due to the high configurational entropy and reactive elemental diversity. This dynamic repassivation, promoted by slight phase transformations at the wear interface, creates a self-healing layer that resists corrosion even while undergoing abrasion, reducing overall degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under combined wear and corrosion, the HEA will exhibit a synergistic performance: a lower overall degradation rate compared to the simple additive effects of wear and corrosion observed in isolated tests. The combined effect will show a moderate reduction in both wear depth and corrosion penetration relative to the baseline isolated conditions.
generation.baseline: The baseline performance is defined by the degradation rates observed when the HEA is exposed separately to only mechanical wear or only corrosion.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold for HEAs with similar metastable microstructures and chemical complexity; it may not apply to alloys with dominant intermetallic phases or those optimized only for either wear or corrosion resistance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the reduction in degradation and the specific conditions under which the passive film exhibits optimal reformation remain uncertain and may vary with test parameters (e.g., mechanical load, corrosion electrolyte concentration).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical HEA samples and conduct three sets of experiments: (1) corrosion only in a saline solution, (2) wear only under a controlled sliding test in an inert medium, and (3) simultaneous wear and corrosion (tribocorrosion). Compare the degradation rates (wear depth, pit depth, and mass loss) among these conditions.
measurements: Wear track depth and width (using profilometry or microscopy)
Corrosion pit density and depth (via SEM or optical microscopy)
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., open-circuit potential and potentiodynamic polarization) to assess passive film behavior
Surface analysis (e.g., XPS or TEM) to evaluate passive film composition and microstructural changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the degradation observed in the combined wear and corrosion test is not lower (i.e., shows a simple additive or synergistically higher degradation) than the sum of the isolated effects, and if no evidence of dynamic passive film regeneration is detected in surface analyses, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
